intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember or warns where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and add your own marks beside mine.

sections.title: Rights online: the starting point
sections.big_idea: Digital rights are **ordinary human rights** exercised through networks, and every limit on them must pass one four-step test.
in_plain_words: There is no separate catalogue of digital rights. Free expression covers a WhatsApp forward, privacy covers a biometric record, and the right to food covers a ration card that depends on online authentication. What changes online is scale, speed and who sits in the middle: a telecom operator, a platform, a government database.

Most of these rights may be limited, so the useful question is whether a limit is lawful. Legality, legitimate aim, necessity and proportionality, applied in order, work for almost every case in this deck. A **measure that fails step one fails outright**, however good its aim.

diagram.caption: four families, each with a constitutional home

key_terms.meaning: A person whose right is at stake, including someone who never went online.
The state first, then private intermediaries that carry out orders.
A public, precise law authorises the measure.
No less restrictive measure would do the job.
The harm to the right is in balance with the benefit.

worked_example.title: Run a measure through the test
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a state orders all mobile data cut for a district, with no end date and no published order.
steps: Legality: is there a public, precise law behind it? Assume an order exists, but it is unpublished, so the first step is already weak.
Legitimate aim: public order is an allowed purpose, so this step may pass.
Necessity: would a narrower measure work, such as limiting the area or the time? An open-ended cut across a district suggests yes.
Proportionality: weigh cash transfers, classes and grievance lines lost against the benefit gained.
worked_example.answer: The measure is likely to fail at necessity or proportionality, and the missing publication weakens legality as well.

mistakes: Treating digital rights as a new list of rights. They are existing rights applied to networks, devices and data.
Thinking only the state owes duties. Intermediaries carry out orders and write their own rules too.
Waiting to test a measure until after it hurts the programme. Run the four steps when you first see the measure.

recall.q: What did Resolution 20/8 of 2012 affirm?
recall.a: That the same rights people have offline must also be protected online, in particular freedom of expression.

recall.q: Name the four steps of the limit test, in order.
recall.a: Legality, legitimate aim, necessity, proportionality.

recall.q: Which two UDHR articles does the deck pair?
recall.a: Article 19 on expression and Article 12 on privacy.

recall.q: Give one harm done to a programme and one done by it.
recall.a: Done to it: a shutdown halting cash transfers. Done by it: a beneficiary list leaking.

recall.q: Which Indian case set out legality, legitimate aim and proportionality for privacy?
recall.a: Puttaswamy (2017).

sections.title: Speech and privacy in the Indian Constitution
sections.big_idea: Four judgments set the frame: **Shreya Singhal** on speech, **Puttaswamy** and **Aadhaar** on privacy, **Anuradha Bhasin** on the internet.
in_plain_words: Article 19(2) lists the only grounds on which speech may be restricted, and annoyance is not one of them. That gap decided Shreya Singhal in 2015: section 66A fell because its words were vague and named harms outside the list. The same judgment upheld blocking under 69A and safe harbour under 79.

Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy a fundamental right under Article 21, with a three-part test. The Aadhaar ruling (2018) upheld Aadhaar for welfare and struck down private demands under contract. Anuradha Bhasin (2020) said **indefinite suspension is impermissible** and orders must be published.

left.title: Struck down or limited
items: IT Act s66A, in its entirety

right.title: Upheld
items: IT Act s69A and Blocking Rules 2009

diagram.caption: what each judgment cut and what it kept

key_terms.meaning: The closed list of grounds for restricting speech.
A law too unclear to tell people what is forbidden.
Lawful speech deterred by fear of a vague law.
The part of privacy that governs databases and apps.
A court order or notification that triggers a platform's duty.

worked_example.title: Apply Shreya Singhal
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a police station files a case over a post said to be "grossly annoying" to a local official.
steps: Check the law: section 66A made annoyance an offence, and the Court struck it down in its entirety.
Check Article 19(2): annoyance, inconvenience and offence are not among the listed grounds.
Check the chilling point: a vague law makes people stay silent, which the Court counted as a harm.
Conclude that no prosecution can rest on 66A, which is dead law.
worked_example.answer: A case built on annoyance alone has no valid basis. Other offences, such as defamation, would need their own check.

mistakes: Remembering only that 66A fell. The same judgment upheld 69A and s79, so blocking and takedowns remain lawful in principle.
Believing a private complaint obliges a platform to remove your post. Actual knowledge means a court order or a government notification.
Reading Anuradha Bhasin as an order to restore the internet. The Court set rules for every order and did not order restoration.

recall.q: On what date was section 66A struck down?
recall.a: 24 March 2015, in Shreya Singhal.

recall.q: What did Puttaswamy hold, and when?
recall.a: That privacy is protected as part of the right to life and liberty under Article 21, on 24 August 2017.

recall.q: What did the Aadhaar judgment strike down?
recall.a: The part of section 57 that let a private body demand Aadhaar authentication under a contract.

recall.q: How often must review committees review suspensions under Anuradha Bhasin?
recall.a: Every seven working days.

recall.q: Which neighbour repealed its Cyber Security Act in 2025?
recall.a: Bangladesh, through the Cyber Security Ordinance 2025.

sections.title: Internet shutdowns in South Asia
sections.big_idea: A shutdown is an **operations risk** as well as a speech issue, so plan the fallback before the order arrives.
in_plain_words: A shutdown can be a full blackout, mobile data only, throttling or a platform block. Access Now counted 313 in 2025, the highest it has recorded, and 195 of them were in Asia Pacific. Myanmar had at least 95, India 65 and Pakistan 20. A count measures how often authorities act and says nothing about how many people lost access.

For a programme, ration authentication, cash transfers, data sync, helplines and remote learning all stop together. India's rules now cap an order at 15 days, require a stated area and a published reason, and give a review committee five days. **Written plans beat improvised ones**, because staff cannot reach each other once phones go down.

children.label: Full or regional blackout
items: All mobile and fixed internet off

key_terms.meaning: A deliberate disruption of internet or mobile services by an authority.
Speeds cut so text loads but video and uploads fail.
Access Now's coalition, which counts shutdowns each year.
A body that reviews a suspension order within five days.
An agreed offline route for a function that needs connectivity.

worked_example.title: How long can an order run?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a State Home Secretary orders a suspension for the maximum period the 2024 Rules allow, and the review committee meets on the last allowed day.
steps: The Rules allow at most 15 days per order.
The review committee must meet within five days.
15 − 5 = 10 days remain after the review committee's latest meeting date.
The committee may set the order aside at that meeting, so the order need not run those days.
worked_example.answer: At most 10 days can follow the latest review date, and the committee may end the order at that review.

mistakes: Reading a lower national count as a lower impact. The count does not show how many people each order reached.
Leaving helplines and grievance lines on data channels only. Voice and SMS often survive a data shutdown.
Advising staff to use VPNs or satellite devices without legal advice. They may breach a lawful order.

recall.q: How many shutdowns did Access Now count worldwide in 2025?
recall.a: 313, across 52 countries.

recall.q: How many did India impose in 2025, and in 2024?
recall.a: 65 in 2025, down from 84 in 2024.

recall.q: Which law replaced the Telegraph Act, and which section covers suspension?
recall.a: The Telecommunications Act 2023, section 20.

recall.q: Name the five steps of the shutdown plan.
recall.a: Map, fallback, communicate, document, report.

recall.q: Why does documentation matter?
recall.a: Courts decide on evidence, and a log turns a complaint into a proportionality argument.

sections.title: Blocking, intermediaries and platform rules
sections.big_idea: Four IT Act sections do most of the work, and **section 79 safe harbour** is the lever that turns rules into pressure on platforms.
in_plain_words: Section 69 allows interception, 69A blocking, 69B traffic-data monitoring and 79 sets the conditions for a platform's safe harbour. Blocking under 69A needs reasons in writing, yet the process is confidential, so the affected person may never see the order. Section 79 protects a platform unless it ignores actual knowledge of unlawful content.

The IT Rules 2021 added grievance officers and duties for large platforms, and later amendments brought labels for synthetic content and a three-hour clock in 2026. Courts have pushed back: the fact check unit fell in 2024, while the Sahyog portal challenge failed in 2025. **Preserve evidence first** when your content is removed.

key_terms.meaning: Power to block public access to information, for reasons in writing.
Platform protection from liability for user content, on conditions.
The conditions a platform must meet to keep safe harbour.
A government system for sending removal notices to platforms.
AI-generated or altered material that appears real.

worked_example.title: Work the removal checklist
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a survivor-support page is removed after a notice citing a legal demand.
steps: Preserve: screenshot the notice, the content and the dates, and export the page data.
Identify the basis: ask the platform which law or order it relied on.
Platform appeal: use its appeal route and the India grievance officer.
If a 69A order is cited, ask for a hearing and the order.
If the grievance officer refuses, appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee, then consider a writ petition with a lawyer.
worked_example.answer: Preserve, identify the basis, appeal, ask for a hearing, appeal again, and go to court last. Keep a backup throughout.

mistakes: Appealing before preserving evidence. A deleted notice cannot be recovered later.
Assuming any complaint forces removal. Shreya Singhal read actual knowledge narrowly.
Relying on the Karnataka ruling without checking the appeal. X Corp's appeal was pending in 2026.

recall.q: What does section 69A allow?
recall.a: The Centre may direct blocking of public access to information, for reasons recorded in writing.

recall.q: What did the Bombay High Court decide in Kunal Kamra?
recall.a: The fact check unit amendment was unconstitutional and struck down, on 26 September 2024.

recall.q: What changed under the 2026 amendment on timing?
recall.a: Platforms must act on orders within three hours, down from 36.

recall.q: What did the Karnataka High Court hold on 24 September 2025?
recall.a: It rejected X Corp's petition and upheld notices through the Sahyog portal.

recall.q: What is the first step when content is removed?
recall.a: Preserve the notice, the content and the dates.

sections.title: Surveillance, spyware and facial recognition
sections.big_idea: Surveillance chills participation even without arrests, and **your own data** can be demanded, stolen or shared.
in_plain_words: India has three routes for interception: the Telecommunications Act s20(2), IT Act s69 and s69B. The executive authorises all three and reviews them in its own committees, with no prior judicial approval. In the Pegasus case the Supreme Court refused to accept a bare claim of national security and appointed a technical committee, which found malware on 5 of 29 phones and nothing conclusive.

Facial recognition shows how a tool can drift from one purpose to another without a new law. Chilling effects follow: people stay away from hearings, refuse photographs and avoid support groups. **The safest record is the one never made**, so collect less, restrict access and delete on a schedule.

diagram.caption: the three-question test for any ID requirement

key_terms.meaning: Monitoring or reading communications as they are sent.
Spyware sold to governments, the subject of a 2021 Supreme Court order.
A tool moves to a new use without a new law or order.
Silence caused by the belief one is watched.
Collecting only the data a purpose requires.

worked_example.title: Read the Pegasus numbers
worked_example.setup: The technical committee examined 29 phones. It found malware on 5 and conclusively showed Pegasus on none.
steps: Phones with some malware: 5 of 29.
Share with malware: 5 ÷ 29 = 17.2%.
Phones with no malware found: 29 − 5 = 24.
Phones conclusively shown to carry Pegasus: 0.
worked_example.answer: About 17.2% of phones had some malware, and none was conclusively tied to Pegasus. The report also noted the government did not cooperate.

mistakes: Reading "inconclusive" as "cleared". The committee recorded that the government did not cooperate.
Treating a court order for one purpose as authority for another. Missing children is a different aim from identifying crowds.
Holding GPS points, caste fields or case notes because they might be useful later. Each field needs a purpose.

recall.q: Who appointed the technical committee in the Pegasus case, and when?
recall.a: The Supreme Court, on 27 October 2021.

recall.q: What did the committee find on the 29 phones?
recall.a: Five had some malware, and none was conclusively shown to be Pegasus.

recall.q: What accuracy did Delhi Police report for its system in 2018?
What does surveillance by design mean for an NGO?
recall.a: Data it holds can be demanded by authorities, stolen by attackers or shared by a vendor.

recall.q: From when do the DPDP duties on minimisation and erasure apply?

sections.title: Digital public infrastructure and the divide
sections.big_idea: Shared rails like UPI help, but **access in a survey is not meaningful access** for a woman with no private device.
in_plain_words: Digital public infrastructure means shared systems on which many apps run: Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and ONDC. Ask five questions of any rail: who sets the rules, who hears complaints, what happens on failure, what data it keeps and whether people can opt out. UPI carried 24.07 billion transactions in September 2026, and the same rail brings fraud with slow redress.

Surveys show a gap. NFHS-6 found 64.3% of women aged 15-49 had ever used the internet, against 80.5% of men. GSMA finds women in South Asia 25% less likely to use mobile internet. **Ever used is a low bar**, so a programme should measure use by each woman, with her own device, privacy, language and skills.

diagram.caption: the survey bar is lower than the rights bar

key_terms.meaning: Shared digital systems on which public and private services run.
Instant account-to-account payments run by NPCI.
A wallet of issued documents shared with consent.
An open network linking buyer and seller apps.
Own device, affordable data, language, skills and safety.

worked_example.title: Read the NFHS-6 gaps
worked_example.setup: NFHS-6 reports ever-used internet for adults aged 15-49: women 64.3%, men 80.5%; rural women 58.6%, rural men 77.1%; women in NFHS-5, 33.3%.
steps: National gap: 80.5 − 64.3 = 16.2 percentage points.
Rural gap: 77.1 − 58.6 = 18.5 percentage points.
Women's growth since NFHS-5: 64.3 ÷ 33.3 = 1.93 times.
The rural gap is wider than the national gap.
worked_example.answer: The national gap is 16.2 points and the rural gap 18.5. Women's use almost doubled, yet it still trails men's.

mistakes: Counting a household as connected when one member is. The mother or sister may have no access.
Comparing a GSMA figure from one edition with another. Methods change between reports.
Designing a service as a smartphone app only. Assume about a quarter fewer women can use it, and plan voice, SMS or assisted routes.

recall.q: Name the four rails in the DPI table.
recall.a: Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and ONDC.

recall.q: What are the five governance questions?
recall.a: Who sets the rules, who hears complaints, what happens on failure, what data it keeps, can people opt out.

recall.q: What share of women had ever used the internet in NFHS-6?
recall.a: 64.3%, against 80.5% of men.

recall.q: What does GSMA find for South Asia?
recall.a: Women are 25% less likely than men to use mobile internet.

recall.q: Give two of the five tests of meaningful access.
recall.a: Any two of: own device used privately, affordable data, her language, skills, safety from harassment.

sections.title: Online harms: gender-based violence and children
sections.big_idea: Technology-enabled abuse is covered by **two statutes**, yet most women do not report it, so build the referral path yourself.
in_plain_words: NCRB recorded 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024, with fraud the motive in 72.6% and sexual exploitation in 3,190. Intimate images fall under IT Act s66E and BNS s77, monitoring under BNS s78, explicit material under 67 and 67A, and child material under 67B and POCSO. Section 78 covers a man monitoring a woman, so other cases need other provisions.

Women stay silent for known reasons: family may take her phone, shame, police advice to stay offline and platforms that ignore her language. Each has a matching help. For children, General Comment No. 25 asks for protection and participation together, and the DPDP Act treats under-18s as children from **13 May 2027**.

diagram.root: Online harm: who the law covers
diagram.caption: harm on the left, provision on the right

key_terms.meaning: Stalking, including monitoring a woman's electronic communication.
Capturing or sharing images of a private act without consent.
UN guidance on children's rights in the digital environment.
A parent's or guardian's consent before a child's data is processed.
Saving content, links and times before they are deleted.

worked_example.title: Read the NCRB cybercrime figures
worked_example.setup: NCRB's Crime in India 2024 records 1,01,928 cybercrime cases in 2024 and 86,420 in 2023. Fraud was the motive in 73,987 cases.
steps: Percentage rise: 15,508 ÷ 86,420 = 17.9%.
Cases with sexual exploitation as the motive: 3,190, a small share.
worked_example.answer: Cases rose 17.9%, and fraud made up 72.6% of them. The registered count is lower than what happened.

mistakes: Reading a high state count as a worse state. Better helplines can record more crime.
Applying section 78 to every stalking case. The wording protects women from men.
Waiting until May 2027 to protect children's data. Ask for parental consent and collect the minimum now.

recall.q: How many cybercrime cases did NCRB record in 2024?
Which provision covers monitoring a woman's online activity?
recall.a: BNS section 78, on stalking.

recall.q: Why do women often not report?
recall.a: Fear the family will take her phone, shame, police advice to stay offline, no knowledge of the law, platforms that do not respond in her language.

recall.q: What does DPDP s9 require for children?
recall.a: Verifiable parental consent, and no tracking or targeted advertising, from 13 May 2027.

recall.q: Which date did General Comment No. 25 carry?
recall.a: 2 March 2021.

sections.title: What AI systems are and how they fail
sections.big_idea: AI systems predict from past data, so **they inherit the past's unfairness** unless someone checks the target, the data and the deployment.
in_plain_words: Most AI in public life is a prediction machine: it learns patterns from past records and produces a score, label, match or text for a new case. It works by resemblance. Sort what you meet into scoring, classification, matching and generative systems, and name the rights risk each carries. The decision step is where rights attach.

Bias enters through three doors: the data, the target and the deployment. Obermeyer showed cost standing in for illness, and Gender Shades showed errors hidden in averages. A rare target also misleads: a 95% accurate flag can wrong most of the people it flags. **Contestability must be designed in**, with notice, reasons and review.

diagram.caption: rights attach at the last box

key_terms.meaning: A measurable variable used in place of the thing a model should predict.
A systematic error that falls harder on some groups.
How common the target is, which shapes how often a flag is wrong.
The practical ability to challenge an output.
A reason hidden in a model or a confidential contract.

worked_example.title: A 95% accurate fraud flag
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 2% of 1,00,000 pension claimants are ineligible, and the model is right 95% of the time for both groups.
steps: Correctly flagged ineligible people: 2,000 × 0.95 = 1,900.
Wrongly flagged eligible people: 98,000 × 0.05 = 4,900.
Share of flagged people who are eligible: 4,900 ÷ 6,800 = 72%.
worked_example.answer: About 72% of the 6,800 people flagged are eligible, so an automatic suspension would mostly cut off entitled people.

mistakes: Accepting an average accuracy figure. Ask for error rates by gender, age, caste, disability and district.
Taking a convenient proxy for the truth. Cost stood in for illness in the Obermeyer study.
Treating a flag as a verdict. Put the burden of verification on the department and keep paying meanwhile.

recall.q: What are the three doors for bias?
recall.a: The data, the target and the deployment.

recall.q: What did the Obermeyer algorithm predict?
recall.a: Future health care costs, which stood in for illness.

recall.q: What was the maximum error rate for darker-skinned women in Gender Shades?
recall.a: Up to 34.7%, against 0.8% for lighter-skinned men.

recall.q: In the base-rate example, how many flagged people are wrongly flagged?
What does contestability need?
recall.a: Notice, a plain reason, a human review that can reverse, and continued benefit meanwhile.

sections.title: AI in welfare, work and elections
sections.big_idea: Telangana shows what happens when a flag ends a benefit: **the person must prove they are entitled**, and the errors fall on the poor.
in_plain_words: Samagra Vedika linked records across departments to find ineligible claimants and wrongly matched poor people to assets they did not own. Telangana cancelled more than 1.86 million food security cards between 2014 and 2019. The re-verification ordered by the Supreme Court found at least 7.5% of processed cards wrongly rejected, against the state's claim of under five per cent.

The same logic runs through work and elections. Data labellers earn little and face harmful content. Gig workers are named in the Code on Social Security, which says little about algorithmic deactivation. The Election Commission tightened rules on deepfakes in steps. **Five design rules** carry across: check, notice, publish errors, test on the judged, keep a non-digital route.

key_terms.meaning: Telangana's system linking records across departments.
A field check of cards the system had cancelled.
An algorithm allocating work, setting pay and deactivating accounts.
Labelling data that AI learns from, often poorly paid.
A mark such as AI-Generated required on party material.

worked_example.title: The Telangana error rate
worked_example.setup: Re-verification applications received: 491,899. Processed by July 2022: 205,734. Approved, so wrongly rejected: 15,471.
steps: Share wrongly rejected among processed: 15,471 ÷ 205,734 = 7.5%.
Applications still unprocessed at that point: 491,899 − 205,734 = 286,165.
The 7.5% counts only people who knew to apply and were processed.
It is a floor, since people who gave up appear in no figure.
worked_example.answer: At least 7.5% of processed cards were wrongly rejected, against the state's claim of under five per cent.

mistakes: Quoting 7.5% as the true error rate. It is a minimum that leaves out those who gave up.
Applying the five rules only to governments. An NGO scoring households for a scholarship faces the same risks.
Promoting data work as a digital job without checking pay per hour worked, harmful content and the contract holder.

recall.q: How many cards did Telangana cancel between 2014 and 2019?
recall.a: More than 1.86 million.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court order in April 2022?
recall.a: Telangana to verify in the field all 1.9 million cards deleted since 2016.

recall.q: Name the five design rules.
recall.a: A flag starts a check, give notice and a reason, publish error rates, test on the people judged, keep a non-digital route.

recall.q: What did the ECI require in its 24 October 2025 advisory?
recall.a: Labels such as AI-Generated covering at least 10% of the visible area, and removal within three hours.

recall.q: When did the four Labour Codes come into force?
recall.a: 21 November 2025.

sections.title: Governing AI: the EU, India and global standards
sections.big_idea: Four instruments govern AI, and **only the EU Act binds**; India relies on guidelines plus existing law.
in_plain_words: The EU AI Act sorts systems by risk: unacceptable (banned), high (strict duties), transparency (disclosure) and minimal. Its high-risk list includes access to services and benefits, education and employment. The Omnibus of July 2026 postponed the main high-risk duties to 2 December 2027, so older summaries are out of date.

India's Guidelines of 5 November 2025 say existing laws can govern most uses and propose an AIGG, an expert committee and a Safety Institute. UNESCO and the OECD give shared vocabulary without enforcement. For a South Asian NGO, **the EU list is a useful benchmark**, and the DPDP Act is the main law for AI on personal data from 13 May 2027.

key_terms.meaning: An AI system in a listed sensitive use, with strict duties.
The July 2026 regulation that postponed high-risk duties.
The principles in India's AI Governance Guidelines.
A Rs 10,371.92 crore programme for compute, data and models.
Non-binding principles from 2019, updated in 2024.

worked_example.title: Sort four uses by EU tier
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a programme considers four tools, and you place each one under the EU AI Act.
steps: A chatbot that answers scheme questions: transparency risk, so it must say it is AI.
A credit-scoring tool for microloans: high risk, as access to essential services.
A spam filter: minimal or no risk, with no new rules.
A tool that scores people socially: unacceptable risk, so banned.
worked_example.answer: Chatbot: transparency. Credit scoring: high risk. Spam filter: minimal. Social scoring: banned.

mistakes: Quoting 2 August 2026 for the high-risk rules. The Omnibus moved Annex III to 2 December 2027.
Telling partners the EU list binds in India. Say that you use it as a benchmark by choice.
Assuming the DPDP duties on consent and accuracy already apply. They commence on 13 May 2027.

recall.q: What is the EU AI Act's regulation number?
recall.a: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

recall.q: When were the India AI Governance Guidelines released?
recall.a: 5 November 2025, by MeitY.

recall.q: What is IndiaAI Mission's outlay and GPU target?
recall.a: Rs 10,371.92 crore, with 10,000 or more GPUs.

recall.q: How many member states adopted the UNESCO Recommendation?
recall.a: 193, in November 2021.

recall.q: Which DPDP provision covers accuracy when data drives a decision?
recall.a: Section 8, applying from 13 May 2027.

sections.title: A digital-rights and AI risk assessment for your programme
sections.big_idea: A short assessment, run at **five triggers** and kept on file, turns this deck's questions into named actions.
in_plain_words: Run the assessment when a new tool arrives, existing data gets a new use, a score or flag feeds a decision, a pilot scales up, or an incident happens. Put the programme lead, a data handler, a safeguarding or legal contact and at least two community members in the room. Answer in writing, and turn every no or unsure into an action with an owner.

Part 1 asks rights questions of every tool; part 2 asks AI questions of any model. The decision table converts answers into four outcomes, and **a flag that can end an entitlement without review is unacceptable as designed**. The pension chatbot example shows a team dropping a score and shipping a smaller, safer version.

diagram.caption: each trigger sends you back to the assessment

key_terms.meaning: Structured questions asked before a tool goes live and when it changes.
The programme's record of risks, each with an owner and a date.
A map from answer patterns to proceed, pilot or pause.
A flag can end an entitlement without review.
An event that sends the team back to the assessment.

worked_example.title: Decide for the pension chatbot
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: four of six widows in the workshop use a son's phone. Version one gives information. Version two adds a score for the block office.
steps: Share of widows on a son's phone: 4 ÷ 6 = 66.7%.
Action: add a missed-call voice line and assisted help at self-help group meetings.
Version two's score would be trained on past approvals, which repeats the Obermeyer pattern.
Decision table: a score that can gate entitlement without review is unacceptable as designed.
worked_example.answer: Launch version one after the actions, with a document checklist instead of the score. Rate version two unacceptable as designed.

mistakes: Running the assessment once at launch. The five triggers include scale-up and incidents.
Leaving the community out of the room. At least two members of the served community should attend.
Recording findings without owners. An action with no owner is a discussion.

recall.q: Name the five triggers.
recall.a: New tool, new use, automation, scale-up, incident.

recall.q: What happens to a "no" or "unsure" answer?
recall.a: It becomes an action with an owner and a date in the risk log.

recall.q: What decision does the table give a flag that can end an entitlement without review?
recall.a: Do not deploy; redesign so a flag only triggers a check.

recall.q: What decision for children's data with any gap in consent or security?
recall.a: Pause until fixed.

recall.q: What data retention did the example contract set?
recall.a: Delete chats after 90 days, with no reuse for training.

sections.title: Summing up and where next
sections.big_idea: Remember one method: **test every limit** with legality, aim, necessity and proportionality, then check every score and keep a way back.
in_plain_words: Ten points carry the deck. On rights: the same rights apply online, every limit must pass the test, privacy is fundamental, 66A is dead, indefinite suspension is impermissible and India imposed 65 shutdowns in 2025. On AI: systems inherit the past, check what a score predicts, ask for error rates by group and let a flag start a check.

The glossary and the four short answers help in practice. The answers are general information as of October 2026 and no legal advice, and the law moves often. For next steps, the suggested reading order is Human Rights, Data Protection & the DPDP Act, then GenAI for Practitioners, with **Child Rights first** for any digital programme with children.

key_terms.meaning: A service that carries or hosts others' content.
A direction to block public access to information.
A temporary shutdown of telecom services.
AI-generated or altered content that appears real.
In the EU Act, a system in a listed sensitive use.

worked_example.title: Compare India's shutdown counts
worked_example.setup: Access Now counted 84 Indian shutdowns in 2024 and 65 in 2025.
steps: Fall in count: 84 − 65 = 19.
Percentage fall: 19 ÷ 84 = 22.6%.
The fall is real, yet the count does not show how many people each order reached.
Ask for the area and duration of each order before drawing a conclusion.
worked_example.answer: The count fell by 19, about 22.6%. Read the trend with the level, and ask about reach.

mistakes: Leaving the deck with a list of cases and no method. The four-step test is the method.
Treating the short answers as legal advice. They are general information as of October 2026.
Skipping Child Rights when a digital programme works with children.

recall.q: What does Resolution 20/8 say?
recall.a: The same rights apply offline and online.

recall.q: What can a practitioner say about section 66A?
recall.a: It is dead law, struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015).

recall.q: What is the DPDP core-duty date?
What is the EU high-risk date after the Omnibus?
recall.a: 2 December 2027.

recall.q: Which question should you ask before refusing a department's demand for a beneficiary list?
recall.a: Ask for the law that requires it and the purpose, and take legal advice.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a route map. Twelve sections run from the legal ground (sections 1 and 2) through shutdowns, blocking and surveillance to AI, and end in a risk assessment you can use. If your work is programme design, read sections 3, 9 and 11 first.
notes.4: Read this slide as a translation exercise. Take any right you already know and ask what changes when a network sits in the middle. The right stays the same. What shifts is **who stands between the person and the right**, and that is where you look for duty-bearers.
notes.5: Learn the two articles as a pair: Article 19 covers what you say and read, Article 12 covers what is kept about you. Most digital disputes set one against the other, so when you meet a case, ask which article each side is relying on.
notes.6: Notice the words "without a vote". They mean no member objected to the wording, which is why advocates quote these resolutions even though a resolution is no treaty. Keep the 2016 text on shutdowns ready, because Section 03 uses it.
notes.7: The table gives each family a constitutional home so you can name the right at stake. Pair them: access with Article 19, expression with 19(1)(a), privacy with Article 21, equality with Articles 14 and 21. Economic and social rights run through all four.
notes.8: Sort your programme's risks into two columns: harms done to the programme and harms done by it. The first needs a plan. The second is a duty the organisation owes. Fill in both columns now, because the risk assessment in Section 11 asks for exactly this.
notes.9: Learn the four steps in order: law, aim, necessity, proportionality. **Stop at the first failure**, because a measure with no legal basis fails whatever its purpose. This one test returns in almost every later section, so copy it onto a card now.
notes.10: This slide tells you what the deck leaves out on purpose. Go to Digital Ethics 101 for Aadhaar exclusion, the DPDP deck for compliance and GenAI for Practitioners for daily tool use. Note the date line, and check the date on any rule before you rely on it.
notes.12: Treat the closed list as eight doors. A restriction on speech has to walk through one of them, and the table groups them into six rows. When a news story reports a speech limit, ask which ground the state claims. **Annoyance is missing**, and that gap decides the next case.
notes.13: Two reasons carried the judgment, and you can name them: vagueness and the chilling effect. A criminal law must say in advance what is punishable. Remember the date, 24 March 2015, and the Court's words that the section was struck down in its entirety.
notes.14: Hold both halves of the case together. Section 66A fell, while 69A blocking and the s79 safe harbour stand, with s79(3)(b) read down. So a private complaint alone does not oblige a platform to act. **A court order or a government notification** does.
notes.15: Puttaswamy is the root of every privacy argument in India. Remember three words for what privacy covers: spatial control, decisional autonomy, informational control. For databases and apps the third one does the work. The nine judges overruled two older benches.
notes.16: This is the Indian wording of the four-step test: law, need, proportion. Use it when a scheme asks your programme for beneficiary data. A guideline or office memorandum is no statute, so ask for the law first. Proportion is where arguments usually turn.
notes.17: Keep the two halves of the 2018 ruling apart. Welfare use was upheld, and private demand for Aadhaar under a contract was struck down. Then note what the Court left open: the person whose fingerprint fails. That gap is where your fallback design earns its place.
notes.18: Anuradha Bhasin did not order the internet restored, yet it set rules that bind every suspension order. Remember the directions: publish orders, review every seven working days, review existing orders, revoke those that fall short. **An unpublished order** cannot be challenged.
notes.19: Do not assume one country's rules carry across a border. The four neighbours moved in four directions: Bangladesh recognises internet access as a civic right, Pakistan added a false-information offence, Sri Lanka created a Commission, and Nepal blocked platforms. Check current status before use.
notes.21: Learn the four forms by what they break. A blackout stops everything, mobile data only hits rural users hardest, throttling is easy to deny, and a platform block targets apps. The form also decides your legal route. Voice and SMS may survive, so plan an SMS fallback.
notes.22: Read the three figures as a measure of how often authorities reach for the tool. A shutdown counts per order, so a two-hour exam cut and a long blackout each count once. The count says nothing about how many people lost access.
notes.23: Read the chart with its cautions. Myanmar had at least 95, India 65 (down from 84) and Pakistan 20. India's fall is real, but ask how many people each order reached, which the count cannot show. The 2025 release gives no Bangladesh figure.
notes.24: Pair each stated reason with the proportionality question beside it. An exam shutdown cuts off millions who are not sitting the test, so ask whether invigilation or jammers in exam halls could do the job. Ask the same question of every reason.
notes.25: Use this table as a planning aid for your own programme. List each function that needs a connection, then write the fallback beside it. Voice and SMS numbers often survive a data shutdown. The slide gives no cost figures because no reliable recent Indian estimate exists.
notes.26: Know the chain: the Telecommunications Act 2023 replaced the Telegraph Act, section 20 took effect on 26 June 2024, and the 2024 Rules set the limits. Remember three of them: 15 days at most, a stated area, and a review committee within five days.
notes.27: Run the five steps in order: map, fallback, communicate, document, report. **Write the plan before the phones go down.** Documentation turns a general complaint into a proportionality argument. Ask a lawyer before you advise anyone to work around a lawful order.
notes.29: Memorise four numbers. Section 69 intercepts, 69A blocks, 69B collects traffic data and 79 gives safe harbour. Two let the state act directly, one serves cyber security and one sets the terms for platforms. With these four, most takedown news becomes readable.
notes.30: Read the grounds in 69A against Article 19(2): they track it, which is one reason the Court upheld the section. The weak point is secrecy, since the blocked person may never see the order. If your page vanishes, ask for the order and keep every message.
notes.31: Section 79 is the platform's shield, and **due diligence is the lever** the state pulls to tighten it. Because Shreya Singhal read actual knowledge narrowly, a complaint alone does not trigger removal. Remember that when mass reporting hits a women's rights page.
notes.32: Sort the 2021 Rules into duties that help users and duties that raise concerns. Use the first set when a complaint arrives: the grievance officer and removal of intimate images. Treat the second set as live legal disputes, especially the originator rule for messaging apps.
notes.33: Follow the dates: a split bench on 31 January 2024, the third judge on 20 September, the decision on 26 September 2024. The lesson is that **the state cannot judge truth about its own business**, and undefined words like fake fail the way section 66A did.
notes.34: Two changes from February 2026 touch you. Label any synthetic images or voices in your awareness material, and know that platforms must now act on orders within three hours, down from 36. The amendments were notified on 10 February and took effect on 20 February.
notes.35: Treat this ruling as live and contested. A single judge held that notices through the Sahyog portal under s79(3)(b) are lawful, and that a foreign company cannot use Article 19. Your content may go on a notice you never see. Check the appeal first.
notes.36: Use the table as an escalation ladder, steps one to six. Step one comes first for a reason: **preserve the evidence**. Then find the legal basis, appeal to the platform, ask for a hearing if 69A is cited, go to the appellate committee, and last go to court.
notes.38: Remember the shape: three routes, all run by the executive, none needing a judge's approval first. That explains the Pegasus case, since a person under surveillance cannot know of it and so cannot challenge it. The slide also lists what the law lacks.
notes.39: The key move is the Court appointing its own technical committee after the government would not answer on affidavit. Keep the principle: the state may withhold what would harm security but must justify the refusal. A bare mention of national security does not end review.
notes.40: Read the three counts together: 29 phones examined, 5 with some malware, 0 shown to be Pegasus. The committee also recorded that the government did not cooperate. The practical lesson is that proof is hard, so update phones and protect high-risk colleagues.
notes.41: Watch the purpose drift. A court order about missing children became the stated base for identifying people elsewhere, including at protests. The reported accuracy was 2% in 2018 and under 1% in 2019. Under Puttaswamy a tool needs a law, and none covers police facial recognition.
notes.42: A chilling effect is a harm that never shows in an arrest count. Look for it in your own data: low turnout at hearings, refusal to be photographed. The remedies are design choices: collect less, say who sees the data, use encrypted channels, offer anonymous routes.
notes.43: Do this exercise on your own data. For each row, ask how it could be misused and choose the safer design. The safest record is the one never made. Remember the date: the DPDP duties on minimisation, security and erasure apply from 13 May 2027.
notes.44: Use the three questions as a design test for any ID rule: is proof needed at all, how little data from it, and what happens when it fails. If a lighter proof would meet the aim, the requirement fails the proportion step as a matter of design.
notes.46: Think of DPI as shared rails. The table names four, who runs each and the rights question attached. The common thread is governance: who sets the rules, who hears complaints, and what happens to people who cannot use the rail.
notes.47: UPI brings a benefit and a risk. The figures show September 2026 volume and value, and the slide pairs cheap transfers and an income record with fraud and slow redress. Link it to Section 07, where fraud is the motive in 72.6% of recorded cybercrime.
notes.48: Keep one word for each rail: consent for DigiLocker, small-seller gain for ONDC. Both are opt-in for users. Watch for a scheme that makes either a condition of a benefit, because that turns a convenience into a gate. Use the latest ONDC release for figures.
notes.49: Use these five questions as a quick audit of any scheme portal or your own beneficiary app. For each one, compare "what good looks like" with the warning sign. The failure question matters most: a manual fallback written into the scheme rules is the strongest protection.
notes.50: Read the gaps as well as the headline. Women's internet use almost doubled to 64.3%, against 80.5% for men, and the rural gap is wider at 58.6% to 77.1%. "Ever used" is a low bar, so treat these as the ceiling of real access.
notes.51: Read the caveat first. The survey is built for national estimates, and a household counts as connected when any member is. So 86.3% of households connected says little about a mother or daughter. Sending an attachment is a basic skill; filling a form is harder.
notes.52: Plan around the 25%. If a service reaches women only through a smartphone app, expect about a quarter fewer women than men to use it, and more in rural areas. Use the current GSMA edition because methods change. Design a voice, SMS or assisted route from the start.
notes.53: Use the five tests as a checklist for any digital service: own device used privately, affordable data, her language, skills, safety. A woman who must ask her husband to file her pension form has access in the survey sense only. Pick two actions from the right-hand list.
notes.55: Remember both sides of the count. Fraud is 72.6% of cases, and sexual exploitation is 3,190, a small share but a large harm. The count shows what police registered. A high figure can mean better access to justice, so compare states with care.
notes.56: Use the table as a lookup from harm to provision. Intimate images: IT Act 66E and BNS 77. Monitoring: BNS 78. Explicit material: IT Act 67 and 67A. Children: 67B and POCSO. Impersonation: 66D. The BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.
notes.57: Teach this section to staff. A partner who tracks her messages or demands her passwords may be committing stalking. Add a phone check to safety planning: unknown apps, shared accounts, location sharing, PIN. Note the gender limit, which sends other cases to other provisions.
notes.58: Treat the two lists as a referral pathway, with a help matched to each reason for silence. Start with a trained private contact and quick platform reporting, then lawyers and the cybercrime portal. Preserve evidence before deletion. The IT Rules route can run beside a police case.
notes.59: General Comment 25 asks states to balance protection and participation, guided by a child's evolving capacities. Blocking every risk would cut children off from learning and from help, so match safeguards to age. Children were consulted when the Committee drafted it.
notes.60: Remember the date. Section 9, with parental consent and no tracking or targeted ads, applies from 13 May 2027 and is not in force today. Under 18 counts as a child. The slide still advises acting early: collect the minimum and ask for parental consent now.
notes.61: Turn each risk into a rule your staff can follow: group channels with two adults, no faces or locations of at-risk children, app reviews before use, a written disclosure route, sessions designed with children. Name who checks each rule, as the third column does.
notes.63: Walk the five boxes left to right: data, training, model, output, decision. The first four happen inside the system. The fifth is where a person or rule acts, and where rights attach. Always ask who acts on the output and whether they can override it.
notes.64: Sort any AI tool into one of four kinds by what it produces. Scoring and classification systems decide more about poor people's lives than generative AI does. Learn the main rights risk for each: exclusion, false positives, wrong matches, confident wrong answers.
notes.65: Use the three doors as questions for a vendor: whose records trained it, what exactly does the score predict, where was it tested and who can override it. Put them into procurement terms. A vendor who cannot answer has not done the work.
notes.66: The lesson is the proxy. Cost stood in for illness, and less had been spent on Black patients, so they scored lower. Hold the two figures, 17.7% flagged against 46.5% if the gap were fixed. Ask of any score what it predicts and whose history it records.
notes.67: Averages hide failing groups. The systems looked accurate overall, yet maximum error was 0.8% for lighter-skinned men and up to 34.7% for darker-skinned women. Before any face-based tool is used on participants, ask for error rates by gender, age and skin tone.
notes.68: Work through the table with a pencil. Of 6,800 people flagged, 4,900 are eligible, about 72%. A rare target makes even a 95% accurate model wrong on most of its flags. The fix is simple: a flag starts a check and payment continues while it runs.
notes.69: Contestability has to be designed in. List the four needs: notice, a plain reason with the data used, a human who can reverse, and continued benefit meanwhile. Article 14 and natural justice give these a legal footing in India even without an AI statute.
notes.71: Telangana shows an automated match treated as truth. A widow was matched to a car owner with a similar name. More than 1.86 million cards were cancelled between 2014 and 2019. The burden fell on the person to prove entitlement, and that pattern is the thing to look for.
notes.72: Read the 7.5% as a floor. Of 205,734 processed applications, 15,471 were approved, so they had been wrongly rejected. The figure leaves out people who never applied or gave up. Compare it with the state's claim that wrong matches stayed under five per cent.
notes.73: Memorise the five rules: a flag starts a check, give notice and a reason, publish error rates, test on the people judged, keep a non-digital route. They apply equally to an NGO that scores households for a scholarship. Find the one your programme is closest to breaking.
notes.74: Data work is real work. The slide gives pay of US$1.32 to 2 an hour for Kenyan workers, platform growth from 142 to 777, and the ILO finding that half of platform workers earn under US$2. Before promoting such jobs, check pay per hour worked, exposure to harmful content and who holds the contract.
notes.75: The Code on Social Security names gig and platform workers for the first time and provides for schemes under s114, with aggregator contributions of 1 to 2% of turnover, capped at 5% of what is paid to these workers. Detail sits in rules, and the Code says little on algorithmic deactivation.
notes.76: Read the table as three tightening steps: a labelling advisory in January 2025, a 10% label and three-hour removal in October 2025, platform instructions with a three-hour clock in April 2026. With no election-specific AI statute, the Model Code and IT Rules do the work.
notes.77: Use the five steps in order: save, report, complain, correct, support. Preserve first, because the content may be deleted. The correction should come from a trusted voice without reposting the fake. Remember that the person targeted carries most of the harm.
notes.79: Tell the four instruments apart with one question: is it binding? The EU AI Act is. India's Guidelines are not, though existing laws are. UNESCO and the OECD are not. A South Asian organisation may meet all four, depending on its donors, users and vendors.
notes.80: Learn the EU tiers by their rule: banned, strict duties, disclosure, none. The Act regulates by use, so one model may land in different tiers. The high-risk list covers access to services and benefits, education and employment, which are your programme areas.
notes.81: Do not quote older summaries that say 2 August 2026 for the high-risk rules. The 2026 Omnibus moved Annex III systems to 2 December 2027 and Annex I products to 2 August 2028. Keep this table beside your policy and note the date you read it.
notes.82: Three routes bring the EU Act to you: donors, vendors and research partners. Where it has no legal force, use its high-risk list and duties as a benchmark, and write in your policy that this is a choice, so staff know which standard binds them.
notes.83: Remember the position: existing laws can govern most AI uses, so India has no separate AI law for now. Learn the seven sutras, and note the third favours innovation. The proposed bodies are the AIGG, an expert committee and an AI Safety Institute. It is guidance, so nothing in it binds.
notes.84: The IndiaAI Mission is public money for compute, data and models. Hold two figures: Rs 10,371.92 crore and 10,000 or more GPUs. Then ask the slide's questions about consent for training data, testing on dialects and women's and Dalit speakers, and who audits the audit tools.
notes.85: UNESCO (2021, 193 states) and the OECD (2019, updated 2024) give a shared vocabulary that does not depend on national law. Neither gives a harmed person a remedy. Cite them when you write an organisational AI policy that donors will recognise.
notes.86: Read the last column. Every duty that matters for AI applies from 13 May 2027, while the Data Protection Board has existed since 13 November 2025. Do not tell partners the research exemption is in force. Use the table to plan which system needs consent, accuracy checks or parental consent.
notes.88: Run the assessment at five triggers: new tool, new use, automation, scale-up and incident. Put at least two people from the community in the room. A half-day suits a small tool; a scoring system needs a test on real cases first. Keep the answers on file.
notes.89: Turn every "no" or "unsure" into an action with an owner and a date in the risk log. The section column tells you where to read when you are stuck. Answer in writing. This half applies to every digital tool, with or without AI.
notes.90: These questions concern the model: what it predicts, on whose data, error rates by group, who can override it, whether people get notice and a reason, and what happens during review. A vendor who cannot answer is itself a finding, so write it down.
notes.91: Convert the answers into one of four decisions. The strictest row is "unacceptable as designed", for a flag that can end an entitlement without review. That is a design verdict, and redesign usually saves the project. Record the decision and the reasons.
notes.92: Notice that the chatbot has two versions. Version one gives a widow information. Version two passes a judgment about her to an authority. The assessment treats them as two different tools. Every name and figure in this example is invented for teaching, so never quote it.
notes.93: Follow each finding across to its action and owner. Study the score trained on past approvals, which repeats the Obermeyer pattern, so the team dropped it. Note that four of six widows use a son's phone, which breaks any assumption of privacy.
notes.94: Watch the final trade. Version two promised more and risked cutting off an entitled widow, so the team launched a smaller version one. The four indicators and four review triggers keep the decision alive after launch. Copy that structure for your own tool.
notes.96: Use this slide for revision: five points on rights online, five on AI. If you remember one method, make it the four-step test of legality, legitimate aim, necessity and proportionality. It works on a shutdown order, a takedown, a surveillance request and an eligibility algorithm.
notes.97: Use the glossary for terms with a legal meaning. Intermediary, safe harbour, blocking order and suspension each trace to a section, and you should quote the section when you write to a department. Be able to explain proportionality and proxy without notes.
notes.98: These four answers are starting points, general information as of October 2026 and no legal advice. The one to remember concerns data demands: ask for the law that requires it and the purpose, because without a law Puttaswamy's first step fails. Take legal advice before refusing.
notes.99: Choose your next course by job. Anyone running a digital programme with children should read Child Rights first. The suggested order is Human Rights, then Data Protection & the DPDP Act, then GenAI for Practitioners. Use the two lists to find deeper material.
